skills.name: Distinguish heat from temperature and measure temperature

note.text:
Heat is energy that flows from a hotter body to a cooler one, measured in joules (J).
Temperature is the degree of hotness of a body, measured in degrees Celsius (°C) or kelvin (K). It decides which way heat flows.
Two bodies at the same temperature can hold very different amounts of heat energy: a bucket of water at 40 °C holds much more than a cup at 40 °C.
When two bodies are in contact, heat flows from the hotter to the cooler until both reach the same temperature: thermal equilibrium.
Kelvin scale: T(K) = θ(°C) + 273. Absolute zero is 0 K = −273 °C. A change of 1 °C equals a change of 1 K.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text:
By the end, you should be able to tell heat from temperature, say which way heat flows, and change between °C and K.
Builds on: Form Three measurement of temperature and the kelvin conversion.
Leads to: Lesson {2} (thermometers) and Lesson {3}, where heat energy is calculated from a temperature change.

sections.heading: Two different ideas
sections.text:
Heat is energy on the move. It flows from a hotter body to a cooler one and is measured in joules.
Temperature is the degree of hotness. It is measured in °C or K, and it decides which way heat flows.
A cup of water at {40} °C and a bucket of water at {40} °C are equally hot, but the bucket holds far more heat energy, because it has many more particles each carrying energy.
Put a hot spoon in cool water: the spoon cools, the water warms, and they meet at one temperature. That is thermal equilibrium: no temperature difference, so no net flow of heat.

sections.heading: The kelvin scale
sections.text:
The Celsius scale takes the melting point of ice as {0} °C and the boiling point of water as {100} °C.
The kelvin scale starts at absolute zero, the lowest temperature possible: {0} K = −{273} °C.
• T(K) = θ(°C) + {273}: {27} °C = {300} K.
• θ(°C) = T(K) − {273}: {350} K = {77} °C.
The two scales have the same size of degree, so a temperature CHANGE is the same number in both: a rise of {20} °C is a rise of {20} K. Do not add {273} to a difference.

key_words.meaning: energy that flows because of a temperature difference, measured in joules
the degree of hotness of a body, in °C or K
the state when two bodies in contact are at the same temperature

examples: a rise from {20} °C to {50} °C is a rise of {30} K

mistake.wrong: a rise of {30} °C is a rise of {303} K
mistake.right: a rise of {30} °C is a rise of {30} K
mistake.why: The {273} is added to a temperature, not to a change. It cancels when you subtract two temperatures.

worked_example.problem: A patient's temperature is {c + 2} °C. Give this temperature in kelvin, and find the rise from {c} °C.
steps: A change of {1} °C is a change of {1} K, so the rise is also {2} K.

cards.idea: Heat is energy in transit, measured in joules. Temperature is the degree of hotness, in °C or K.
example: A bucket and a cup of water at {40} °C are equally hot, but the bucket holds more heat energy

cards.idea: Heat flows from hot to cold until the temperatures are equal (thermal equilibrium).
example: A hot spoon in cold water cools; the water warms; they meet at one temperature

check.prompt: A metal spoon at {hot} °C is put into water at {cold} °C. What happens?
check.correct: Heat flows from the spoon to the water until both are at the same temperature

distractors.text: Heat flows from the water to the spoon
Nothing happens until the spoon melts
Both stay at their own temperature

misconceptions.explain: The water is cooler, so it takes in heat; it does not give heat to the hotter spoon.
Heat flows as soon as two bodies at different temperatures touch.
A temperature difference always causes a flow of heat.

solution: Heat always flows from the hotter body to the cooler one.
The spoon at {hot} °C is hotter than the water at {cold} °C.
They stop exchanging heat when they reach the same temperature.
So the answer is: {answer}.

pick.q: Which statement about heat and temperature is correct?
pick.r: Heat is energy that flows; temperature tells how hot something is
w: Heat and temperature mean the same thing
A bigger object always has a higher temperature
e: They are different: heat is energy in transit (joules); temperature is the degree of hotness (°C or K).
Size does not fix temperature: a cup and a bucket of water from the same tap are equally hot.
Temperature is measured in degrees Celsius or kelvin; heat is measured in joules.
pick.y: Heat is energy that flows from a hotter body to a cooler one; temperature decides which way it flows.

pick.q: A cup of tea and a bucket of water are both at 40 °C. Which holds more heat energy?
pick.r: The bucket, because it has more particles
w: The cup, because it feels hotter
They hold the same, because the temperature is the same
e: They are at the same temperature, so neither feels hotter; the bucket simply holds more energy.
Equal temperature does not mean equal energy: the bucket has far more particles, each with energy.
Any body above absolute zero has internal energy.
pick.y: At the same temperature each particle has the same average energy, so more particles means more energy in all.

pick.q: Two objects touch. Which way does heat flow?
pick.r: From the hotter one to the cooler one
w: From the bigger one to the smaller one
From the cooler one to the hotter one
Heat does not flow between touching objects
e: Size does not decide the direction; the temperature difference does.
Heat always flows the other way, from hot to cold, until the temperatures are equal.
Touching bodies at different temperatures always exchange heat.
pick.y: Heat flows from high to low temperature until both reach the same temperature (thermal equilibrium).

pick.r: Two bodies in contact have reached the same temperature
w: Both bodies hold the same amount of heat energy
One body has no heat energy left
The bodies have the same mass
e: Equal temperature, not equal energy: a large body at the same temperature still holds more energy.
A body at any temperature above absolute zero still has internal energy.
Mass has nothing to do with it.
pick.y: At thermal equilibrium there is no temperature difference, so no net flow of heat.

pick.q: Which temperature scale starts at absolute zero?
w: Every scale starts at absolute zero
e: Celsius starts at the melting point of ice, which is 273 K.
Fahrenheit has its own fixed points; it does not start at absolute zero.
Only the kelvin scale has its zero at absolute zero.
pick.y: 0 K is absolute zero, the lowest possible temperature; T(K) = θ(°C) + 273.

questions.prompt: Water in a kettle is heated from {a} °C to {b} °C. What is the rise in temperature, in kelvin?

misconceptions.explain: A temperature CHANGE is the same number in °C and K: do not add {273} to a difference.
Change both to kelvin and the {273} cancels: ({b} + {273}) − ({a} + {273}) = {b - a}.

solution: The rise is {b} − {a} = {b - a} °C.
A change of {1} °C is a change of {1} K, so the rise is {answer} K.

questions.prompt: A cup holding {m1} g of water and a pot holding {m2} g of water are both at {t} °C. Which statement is true?
questions.correct: The pot holds more heat energy, because it has more water at the same temperature

distractors.text: The cup holds more heat energy, because it is hotter
They hold the same heat energy, because the temperature is equal

misconceptions.explain: Both are at {t} °C: neither is hotter.
Equal temperature means equal average energy per particle, not equal total energy.
Any body above absolute zero (−{273} °C) has internal energy.

solution: Both are at {t} °C, so their particles have the same average energy.
The pot has {m2 / m1} times as much water, so many more particles.
So the pot holds more energy in all.
So the answer is: {answer}.
